rationale: A wins because it gives the founder real press strategy, not just angle-shaped summaries. A's sharpest line, "Bumble's AI writes the opening message on the app built around who sends it," finds the internal contradiction and tells you exactly what proof would make it stand up; B's parallel, "Bumble keeps women-message-first as it hands message-writing to AI," is valid but looser and slightly more slogan-shaped. B is usable, but A is the one that knows where the bodies are buried before a reporter starts digging.
gaps_in_A: "the first substantive product move since the founder's return this year" is stronger than the fact block supports; the update says the relaunch is under the returning founder-CEO, not that it is her first substantive move.

"Dating apps are selling AI to users who say AI ruins dating" overstates the plural trend before proving other dating apps are doing the same; A catches this in proof, but the headline still gets ahead of the evidence.
gaps_in_B: "the Dorsey/Schultz/Kalanick-adjacent storyline" is a lazy comparison cluster and drags in baggage the fact block did not earn.
"A tech-business feature reporter at a national outlet" is still a little broad; A more cleanly defines desk, exclusion, timing, and editorial logic.
"a major public dating company" is defensible, but it adds weight not supplied in the update; public is given, major is implied, not proven.

The refused angles and uncomfortable questions are thinner than A's; B identifies the obvious traps but misses sharper landmines like disclosure to recipients and whether the company wants scrutiny before results exist.
